status2026.detail: On the APS 'Beamline Commissioning Progress' chart dated 5 Oct 2026, '20-ID-D,E: HEXM XSD' is at stage 6, 'Restart of General User Program'. The APS Proposal Types page (dated 10.07.2026) lists 20-ID-D,E among beamlines taking General User regular and rapid-access proposals. How it got there, from the monthly charts: stage 1 (installation ongoing) on 30 Sep 2024; stage 2 (installation complete) on 16 Dec 2024 and in Jan 2025; stage 3 (ops commissioning) on 10 Mar 2025; stage 5 (scientific commissioning and early experiments) from Jul 2025 through Jan 2026. In July 2025, Energy Secretary Chris Wright placed an 'inaugural sample', part of a jet-engine turbine blade, in the HEXM instrument. A July 2025 NSUF/APS report says the beamline 'achieved shielding verification in 2025' and expected general users in late 2025 or early 2026. The first-light date was not published: the charts bracket it between late January and July 2025, probably by March if stage 3 already involved beam-on shielding verification (not confirmed). The September 2024 update had expected first light in that run; the charts show this did not happen in 2024. Caveats: (1) the Beamline Directory entry (re-read 2026-10-09) still says 'Current Status: Commissioning', and its specs assume a superconducting undulator; it warns they 'will not be fully valid during the startup of the beamline, which could last ~year'. (2) The source is still an interim pair of permanent-magnet undulators: U21 upstream and a U21/U25 revolver downstream (APS insertion-device table, updated 22 Sep 2026, re-read 2026-10-09). The baseline in-line superconducting undulator pair (2 × 1.9 m, 16.5 mm period) was delayed by SCU core-reliability problems and is planned for 2026–2027. The Strategic Plan schedule shows 20-ID SCU core fabrication through 2026–2027 and commissioning around late 2027; its May 2026 target for the first in-line SCU (sector 1) had not been met by the 22 Sep 2026 ID table, which lists no SCU at sector 1 or 20. (3) The adjacent Activated Materials Laboratory is operational. A Partner User Proposal gives NSUF 690 h/yr shared between 1-ID and 20-ID, starting in the 2025-3 run. HEXM was already absent from the August 2025 list of the 'last five feature beamlines' still to come online.

tagline: A 180-metre X-ray microscope that sees deep inside solid metal, from whole samples down to the spacing of atoms.
summary: The X-rays used at most beamlines are stopped by steel as thin as a sheet of paper. The High-Energy X-ray Microscope (HEXM) uses X-rays of 35–120 keV (35,000 to 120,000 electron-volts) that pass through millimetres of metal, so scientists can watch the inside of a jet-engine alloy, a battery or reactor steel while it is pulled, heated or charged. The beam travels about 180 m to the sample in 20-ID-E, a room nearly 20 m long in its own building. The distance serves two opposite ends: the beam can be spread to several millimetres to see a whole sample, or, in the design, focused to a spot about 200 nm tall to study one crystal grain. Detectors from a centimetre to 16 m behind the sample show how thousands of grains turn and stretch, and where cracks begin. A laboratory next door prepares radioactive samples from nuclear reactors. HEXM is open to general users but still runs on stand-in undulators.

whatAPSUEnables.text: In the design's brightness mode, the upgraded ring's electron beam is about 19 times narrower from side to side (14.7 µm root-mean-square width instead of 280 µm), and its vertical emittance, size times angular spread, falls from about 40 to 4 pm·rad. That pays off most at high energies, where the light's own spread is small and the electron beam sets the source. Over 180 m, lenses 2 m before the sample can shrink that tiny source to a spot designed to be about 200 nm tall, leaving room for furnaces and load frames, or the nearly parallel beam can be spread over several millimetres. Before the upgrade only about 1 photon in 100,000 at these energies was coherent, its waves in step: too few for lens-free imaging of strain inside single grains. The design projects about 500 times the coherent flux of the old 1-ID at 40 keV, but it assumes superconducting undulators not yet installed; no measured values are published.
quantitative: Horizontal emittance: 3,113 pm before the upgrade → 42 pm on APS-U (brightness mode), about 74× smaller; horizontal rms source size 280 → 14.7 µm.

Nominal electron-beam parameters at the ID straight from the design-lattice model (flat-beam mode, zero current; computed values, not measurements): σx = 14.5 µm, σx′ = 2.75 µrad, σy = 3.08 µm, σy′ = 1.29 µrad.
The coherent fraction at HEDM energies was about 10⁻⁵ before the upgrade, too low for high-energy coherent diffraction imaging.
Projected gains at 40 keV over pre-upgrade 1-ID: about 500× in coherent flux and 150× in coherent fraction.
Smallest design focus at 20-ID-E: 0.43 × 0.21 µm FWHM at 70 keV with 4 × 10¹¹ ph/s (f = 2 m, L6); below 100 nm vertically is projected with an f = 1 m kinoform.

Largest beams: 2.5 × 2.2 mm FWHM unfocused at 180 m (70 keV), or several mm with refractive expanders. Sample cross-sections 'were one millimeter before. Now they can be up to several millimeters' (Almer).
SAXS: Qmin = 0.0007 Å⁻¹ at 40 keV (dmax about 870 nm), a 6× larger observable range than at 1-ID-E.
Scattering-tomography resolution is set by the beam size: about 2 µm before, about 0.1 µm planned.
The planned SCU vs the pre-upgrade SCU1 at 1-ID: 530× the brilliance, 4.5× the central-cone flux, and 1.5× the flux density even after moving from 70 m to 180 m.
Expected data rates are about 100× those of 1-ID before the upgrade.

techniques.name: Far-field high-energy diffraction microscopy
techniques.text: A metal is a jigsaw of many small crystals, or grains, and each throws a few sharp diffraction spots whenever it sits at just the right angle to the beam. Far-field high-energy diffraction microscopy (ff-HEDM, also called 3DXRD) rotates the sample in a beam 1–2 mm wide while a flat-panel detector 0.5–1.5 m away records a series of frames, and software assigns every spot to its grain. For up to about 10,000 grains at once, the result is each grain's position, crystal orientation and full elastic strain, how much it is stretched or squeezed along every direction. At the old 1-ID-E the measured repeatability was about 5 µm in position, 0.02° in orientation and 2 × 10⁻⁴ in strain. HEXM runs it in both 20-ID-D and 20-ID-E.

techniques.name: Near-field high-energy diffraction microscopy
techniques.text: Near-field HEDM (nf-HEDM) places a high-resolution camera just 1–2 cm behind the sample, where each diffraction spot still lies close to the grain that made it. A flat 'line' beam, under a micrometre tall and ideally 3–4 mm wide, slices through the sample as it rotates and steps vertically, and the camera records at several distances. Software then finds the grain shapes that would produce the observed spots (forward modelling), giving a 3D map of grains and their boundaries, like a CT scan coloured by crystal orientation, with about 1 µm and 0.01° resolution. HEXM's long beamline lets diamond lenses spread the beam into that wide line efficiently.

techniques.name: Very-far-field HEDM
techniques.text: Very-far-field HEDM (vff-HEDM) moves the detector 10 m or more from the sample, up to about 16 m in 20-ID-E. Strain, a change in the spacing of atoms, shifts each diffraction spot by a tiny angle, tinier still at the small scattering angles of high-energy X-rays, and the farther away the detector, the smaller the angle each pixel covers. That makes strain visible even within a single grain. It also needs a very narrow energy spread, about 10⁻⁴, from the four-bounce monochromator, or the beam's own spread of wavelengths would blur the spots.

techniques.name: Wide-angle X-ray scattering / high-energy diffraction / pair distribution function
techniques.text: Wide-angle scattering, or high-energy diffraction, records the complete rings made by many grains at once, much like weighing a crowd rather than each person. The rings show which crystal phases are present and in what proportions, how hard each is loaded (lattice strain), how the grains are oriented (texture) and, from the width of the peaks, how many defects they contain; a pair distribution function (PDF) analysis turns data out to high scattering angles into the distribution of distances between atoms. Measurements are in transmission, at scattering angles below about 10–18°. For the most photons, white-beam lenses can focus a whole undulator harmonic, 0.6% wide in energy: 4.8 × 10¹⁴ photons per second at 70 keV in the design.

techniques.name: Scattering tomography
techniques.text: Scattering tomography combines a CT scan with diffraction: a pencil-thin beam is scanned across the sample, which is then rotated, and a wide-angle or small-angle pattern is recorded at every step. A computer rebuilds a 3D map of which material, how much strain or what nanostructure sits at each point inside. Its resolution equals the beam size, so HEXM's focusing should take it from about 2 µm before the upgrade toward about 0.1 µm.

techniques.name: High-energy small-angle X-ray scattering
techniques.text: High-energy small-angle X-ray scattering (HE-SAXS) records X-rays deflected by tiny angles, which reveal nanometre-scale voids, precipitates and fibres: features too small to see directly but important for strength. With the detector about 14 m downstream, the design reaches a smallest scattering vector of 0.0007 Å⁻¹ at 40 keV, corresponding to structures up to about 870 nm, six times the range of the old 1-ID-E. For the first time that range overlaps with what the high-energy X-ray microscope can image directly, so the same voids or particles can be measured both ways.

techniques.name: Micro-computed tomography (absorption and phase contrast)
techniques.text: Micro-computed tomography (µCT) is a 3D X-ray scan, like a hospital CT but with micrometre detail, showing pores, cracks and second phases inside dense parts. The camera images the whole illuminated field at once and, as a rule of thumb, resolves about a thousandth of the beam's width, so beam size sets the trade-off between volume and detail. An expanded white beam, or a single undulator harmonic, can give datasets with about 1 µm resolution in a fraction of a second. The more coherent beam also strengthens phase contrast, which shows edges by how they bend the X-ray wave rather than by how much they absorb.

techniques.name: High-energy transmission X-ray microscopy
techniques.text: A transmission X-ray microscope (TXM) works like a slide projector: an X-ray lens placed after the sample casts a magnified image onto a camera about 15 m away. Because a lens does the magnifying rather than the camera's pixels, it can resolve details much finer than an ordinary CT scan. At the old 1-ID the method reached about 500 nm resolution at 45 keV within 6 m; HEXM's longer room allows higher magnification and depth of field, with a goal of about 100 nm.

techniques.name: Bragg coherent diffraction imaging (high-energy)
techniques.text: Bragg coherent diffraction imaging (BCDI) lights a single buried grain with a coherent beam, one whose waves are in step across the grain. Its diffraction spot then becomes a 3D speckle pattern, from which a computer recovers the grain's shape and the tiny displacements of its atoms, revealing strain inside it, with a goal of tens-of-nanometre detail. HEXM's design uses a 48 × 31 µm coherent focus at 40 keV with an energy spread of only 2 × 10⁻⁶, for grains up to about 10–20 µm; grains are chosen from a far-field grain map (ff-HEDM) and their patterns recorded about 16 m away. A proof of principle at 52 keV at the old 1-ID-E imaged structures of about 0.5 µm or smaller with a strain resolution of about 2.5 × 10⁻⁴.

techniques.name: Dark-field X-ray microscopy
techniques.text: Dark-field X-ray microscopy (DFXM) is a microscope tuned to one crystal: an objective lens placed in the beam diffracted by a single grain projects a magnified image made only by that grain's X-rays. Tiny tilts and strains inside the grain change how strongly each part diffracts, so the image maps orientation and strain at better than a micrometre, deep inside bulk material. HEXM has been described as 'the only beamline worldwide to offer dark-field X-ray microscopy at high energies' (A. Bucsek), but this is a planned or emerging mode: no published HEXM result has been found.

scienceCases.title: Why turbine alloys crack: dwell fatigue in Ti and Ni superalloys
scienceCases.text: Jet-engine parts can crack after many cycles of stress that include long holds under load, a failure called dwell fatigue: in titanium alloys even at room temperature, in nickel superalloys above about 700 °C. HEXM can map around a thousand grains inside a real alloy sample under load and heat, find the few 'hot spot' grains where strain piles up, then zoom in on them with coherent imaging, dark-field microscopy or CT to see where voids and cracks begin. The aim is to test the idea that some slip systems, the planes along which a crystal shears, slowly creep while others respond as they would at low temperature. Fittingly, the inaugural sample, placed by Energy Secretary Chris Wright in July 2025, was part of a jet-engine turbine blade.

scienceCases.title: Inside irradiated nuclear materials
scienceCases.text: Steel and fuel from nuclear reactors become radioactive, which makes them hard to study. The Activated Materials Laboratory next to 20-ID-E, funded through the Nuclear Science User Facilities (NSUF), prepares and seals samples giving up to 100 millirem per hour at 30 cm, and HEXM's penetrating X-rays then map cracks, voids and grain strains in 3D, with heating and loading in place. NSUF holds 690 hours a year shared between 1-ID and 20-ID, and the more radioactive samples are meant to go mainly to 20-ID because it sits outside the main hall. The first user experiment examined stainless steel retired from a light-water reactor after decades of service, seeking grain-level clues to irradiation-assisted stress-corrosion cracking; which beamline it used was not stated.

scienceCases.title: Additive manufacturing: pores, residual stress and grains in 3D-printed metal
scienceCases.text: 3D-printed metal parts can hide tiny pores and locked-in (residual) stresses. HEXM's large-field CT, with resolution planned down to about 100 nm, can find small pores in volumes big enough to be statistically meaningful, while high-energy diffraction microscopy (HEDM) measures each grain's orientation and residual strain and small-angle scattering (SAXS) finds nanoscale precipitates. Experiments during printing or welding are planned, with real-time analysis feeding back to narrow down which process settings are worth trying.

scienceCases.title: Batteries that crack as they charge
scienceCases.text: Battery cathode particles are clusters of tiny crystals, each 10–500 nm across, that can crack apart along their boundaries after many charges, because each crystal swells unevenly as lithium moves in and out. HEXM aims to measure the stresses at the level of these individual crystals, using nano-focused diffraction microscopy (HEDM) and coherent imaging on many particles at once inside full-size working cells. A battery cycler is part of the station's equipment, so cells can be charged and discharged during the measurement.

scienceCases.title: Bone and other natural composites
scienceCases.text: Bone is a natural composite of protein fibres about 100 nm wide and mineral crystals. Scattering tomography with small- and wide-angle scattering can map how strain is shared between fibres and mineral when bone is loaded, and HEXM's finer beam should improve its resolution from about 2 µm toward about 0.1 µm. High energies also help with radiation dose: for biological tissue the dose needed for a given image is lowest at about 60–100 keV, between the regimes dominated by photoelectric absorption and by Compton scattering.

scienceCases.title: Grain mapping as a high-throughput service
scienceCases.text: The high-throughput high-energy diffraction microscopy (HEDM) instrument in 20-ID-D was built with a National Science Foundation instrumentation grant by four universities: Carnegie Mellon (the lead), Purdue, Utah and the Colorado School of Mines. A six-axis motorised stage turns and steps each sample through the beam, making grain mapping something like an assembly line, so many more samples can be measured, possibly even mailed in. First installed at 6-ID-D, it moved to 20-ID-D in December 2023. As R. Suter put it: 'Many places with wading pools…this instrument…will be an Olympic swimming pool'.

keyParameters.label: Photon energy (monochromatic)
keyParameters.note: The Beamline Directory gives 35–120 keV; the 2021 D3 detector-mover specification quotes 35–140 keV for the photon delivery system. White beam and focused 'broadband' undulator harmonics are also available.

keyParameters.label: White-beam capability
keyParameters.note: Monochromators and lenses can be moved out of the beam for white-beam operation.

keyParameters.label: Energy resolution ΔE/E
keyParameters.value: 10⁻³ (bent double-Laue); about 10⁻⁴ (four-bounce, Si(111)); 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁶ (four-bounce, high-order Si reflections)
keyParameters.note: The AML report lists the optional high-resolution monochromator as ΔE/E of about 10⁻⁵.

keyParameters.value: 10¹⁴ ph/s (200 mA, brightness mode, planned SCU source)
keyParameters.note: Design value assuming the 16.5 mm SCU. The current interim permanent-magnet source should give less: the Strategic Plan says SCUs boost brightness by about 3× over hybrid permanent-magnet undulators above 50 keV. No measured 20-ID value is published.

insertionDevices.name: APS21#5 (U21), upstream
insertionDevices.notes: 112 periods; device minimum gap 8.5 mm; Keff 1.38 at minimum gap; E1 = 8.36 keV (6.0 GeV, zero emittance); 216 kW/mrad² and 5.4 kW at 200 mA. Length = 112 × 21 mm (the Beamline Directory says '2.3 m length'). Interim source as of 22 September 2026.

insertionDevices.name: APS21R25#9 revolver (U21 / U25), downstream
insertionDevices.type: planar hybrid permanent-magnet revolver undulator (two magnetic structures, selectable)
insertionDevices.notes: Structure 1: APS21#14, 21 mm, 112 periods, K 1.38, E1 = 8.32 keV. Structure 2: APS25#11, 25 mm, 94 periods, K 1.98, E1 = 4.61 keV, 224 kW/mrad², 8.0 kW. The Beamline Directory lists the downstream source as U21. Interim source.

insertionDevices.name: SCU 16.5 mm in-line pair (baseline, not yet installed)
insertionDevices.type: planar superconducting undulator (NbTi), two magnets in one 4.8 m cryostat
insertionDevices.notes: APS-U baseline for sectors 1 and 20: 'two pairs of 1.9-meter-long, 16.5-mm period SCUs in inline configuration', with correctors inside the long cryostat. Installation was delayed by core reliability issues and is now planned for 2026–2027. FDR 4-4 (2019) specified about 3.5 m (possibly 3.8 m) total magnetic length, Kmax 1.63 (1.06 T at 8.0 mm gap), 1.6 kW and 600 kW/mrad² through the 2 × 1 mm mask. PDR: 17.9 kW total and 616 kW/mrad² at max field. A 2020 overview: 'Current undulator lengths are 1.1 m with up to 3.5m planned for the APS-Upgrade'. The 2025–29 Strategic Plan schedule (Fig. 8) shows 20-ID SCU core fabrication through 2026–2027 and commissioning around late 2027. The plan's May 2026 target for the first in-line SCU (sector 1) had not been met by the 22 Sep 2026 ID table, which lists no SCU at sector 1 or 20.

source.canting: None: two in-line devices on one straight, with a phase shifter/corrector between the permanent-magnet devices; for the SCUs, correctors sit inside the cryostat.
source.frontEnd: Standard APS-U High-Heat-Load front end (HHLFE, based on the 28-ID design): total power limit 21 kW, peak power density 590 kW/mrad². Contents: clearing magnet, burn-through fixed mask (BTFM1), GRID XBPM1, photon shutter with intensity monitor, safety shutters, and exit mask with XBPM2. For 20-ID: window exit configuration with a 2 (H) × 1 (V) mm exit mask at 25.4 m and a 5 × 5 mm tungsten exit collimator at 26.1 m. The window material is inconsistent in the FDR: 0.5 mm Be in 4-4.3, diamond in Table 4.28.
source.sourceSizeAndDivergence: Electron beam at the ID straight (APS-U design-lattice model values at zero current, not measurements). Flat-beam mode (used for the brightness-mode design; κ = 0.1): σx = 14.47 µm, σx′ = 2.75 µrad, σy = 3.08 µm, σy′ = 1.29 µrad. Round-beam mode (used for the timing-mode design): σx = 12.3 µm, σx′ = 2.34 µrad, σy = 8.26 µm, σy′ = 3.47 µrad. FDR Table 1.1 design (brightness): 14.7 / 2.8 / 3.2 / 1.3. Computed here, not from a source: at 70 keV for a 2.35 m undulator the single-electron photon size and divergence are about 0.7 µm and 1.9 µrad. That gives total photon source sizes of about 14.5 × 3.2 µm and divergences of about 3.4 × 2.3 µrad rms, before energy-spread broadening, which becomes significant at the high harmonics (7th–13th) HEXM uses. FDR Fig. 4.20 uses 35 µm (H) × 9 µm (V) FWHM source sizes for the BCDI optics design, and the PDR text quotes the same 9 µm vertical FWHM.

branches.name: 20-ID (single branch)
branches.description: One straight beamline with no net horizontal deflection. The bent Laue monochromator displaces the monochromatic beam about 25–35 mm outboard, parallel to the white-beam axis. White or monochromatic beam goes to 20-ID-D (about 70 m) or, through a movable stop, on to 20-ID-E (about 180 m) in the Long Beamline Building.

components.name: Upstream undulator U21 (APS21#5)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: two 2.35 m devices sit in line on the straight, centred on the source point (0 m); device centres are estimated at about ±1.3 m.
components.text: The first of two undulators that make HEXM's X-rays: a 2.35 m row of 224 alternating magnets that makes each passing electron wiggle, so the light from every wiggle adds up into one narrow, bright beam. Its fundamental energy is only 8.36 keV at the smallest gap, rising as the gap opens, so HEXM uses its harmonics, whole-number multiples of that energy: 35 keV on the third, 70 keV on about the seventh and 120 keV on the 11th to 13th. It is an interim permanent-magnet device, a stand-in until superconducting undulators arrive.

components.name: Downstream revolver undulator U21/U25 (APS21R25#9)
components.distanceNote: Approximate (see the upstream device).
components.text: A second undulator right behind the first roughly doubles the light. It is a 'revolver': it carries two magnet rows with different periods, 21 mm or 25 mm, and rotates to put the chosen one around the electron beam; the beamline directory lists the 21 mm row as the source. A phase shifter between the two undulators keeps their light in step. Both are interim: the baseline is a pair of 1.9 m superconducting undulators with a 16.5 mm period in one 4.8 m cryostat, now planned for 2026–2027.

specs.baseline replacement: 2 × 1.9 m, 16.5 mm NbTi SCU in a 4.8 m cryostat

components.name: High-heat-load front end (shutters, masks, XBPMs)
components.distanceNote: Schematic placement inside the storage-ring tunnel. The front end ends at the ratchet wall at about 25.4–26.1 m; exact internal positions are not published.
components.text: The safety gateway between the accelerator and the beamline, inside the concrete shield tunnel. It swallows unwanted X-ray power, checks where the beam points with X-ray beam-position monitors, and can shut the X-rays off in a fraction of a second. It is the standard high-heat-load front end of the upgraded APS, rated for 21 kW; the two undulators at their smallest gap deliver about 10.8 kW.

components.name: Front-end exit mask and window
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: Where the beam leaves the shield tunnel, an opening 2 mm wide and 1 mm tall, half the height of the standard mask, lets only the bright centre of the X-ray cone through and limits the heat on the optics. A thin window then separates the accelerator's vacuum from the beamline's; the design documents disagree on whether it is 0.5 mm of beryllium or diamond, and the as-built choice is unconfirmed.

specs.window: 0.5 mm Be (FDR text) or diamond (FDR table); as-built unconfirmed

components.name: Front-end exit collimator
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: A heavy tungsten block with a 5 mm square hole. It stops bremsstrahlung ('braking radiation'), very-high-energy radiation made when electrons hit gas or metal in the accelerator, from travelling down the beamline alongside the X-rays.

components.name: White-beam filters F1 (20ID-FL-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: Thin sheets of diamond and silicon that soak up the low-energy X-rays, which would only heat the optics downstream, while more than 85% of the useful X-rays at 40 keV pass straight through. Each sheet absorbs under 100 W, and together with the slits they hold the heat on the first monochromator crystal to about 55–60 W, little enough for liquid-nitrogen cooling to handle.

components.name: High-heat-load white-beam slits S1 (20ID-SL-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: Cooled metal jaws with tungsten edges that trim the beam to its bright central core, usually 0.6 mm square or smaller (2 mm at most). That is just enough to pass the whole central cone at 70 keV, slightly broadened by the spread of electron energies in the ring; everything outside the square ends up here as heat.

components.name: L1 white-beam diamond refractive lenses
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: Stacks of small, cooled diamond lenses that act on the beam before any crystal has selected an energy. A lens focuses each energy at a slightly different distance, so it cannot focus the full white beam sharply, but one undulator harmonic, a band only about 0.6% wide, comes to a good focus: by design 4.8 × 10¹⁴ photons per second at 70 keV, four to five times more than a single narrow energy, for the fastest experiments. Swapped by hand, the lenses can instead spread the white beam to several millimetres for imaging.

components.name: M1 high-energy bent double-Laue monochromator (20ID-MN-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28. In the 3D model the two crystals are 0.53 m apart, the spacing that gives a 30 mm offset at 70 keV (computed: 30 mm / tan 2θB); the white-beam stop sits between them on the white-beam axis.
components.text: HEXM's main monochromator: two thin, bent silicon crystals that pick out a single X-ray energy, with a spread of about 0.1%, anywhere from 35 to 120 keV. At these energies the X-rays pass through the crystals rather than bouncing off their surface (Laue geometry), at just 1.6° to the crystal planes at 70 keV, and bending lets the crystals accept a wider range of angles: the predecessor at 1-ID gave more than ten times the flux of flat crystals. The second crystal undoes the distortions of the first, and the pair diffracts sideways, preserving the beam's tiny vertical size and spread; the chosen energy leaves 25–35 mm to the side, parallel to the original beam. Cooled with liquid nitrogen, it was installed in January 2024.

components.name: Diamond window (20ID-WN-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: A thin diamond window that seals off the first vacuum section, from the front-end window through the monochromator, while letting the high-energy X-rays through almost untouched. At these energies a thin sheet of diamond absorbs very little.

components.name: L2 collimating lenses
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28, where the lenses are marked 'not in project scope'.
components.text: Weak lenses that make the beam almost perfectly parallel, with a focal length of about 31 m in the coherent-imaging setup. That matters because the crystals of the next monochromator accept only a tiny range of angles, so a parallel beam passes far more photons. A 2026 paper reports diamond collimating lenses used this way on 'a long beamline', presumably this one; like most of HEXM's lenses, they were outside the upgrade project's scope.

components.name: M2 high-resolution four-bounce monochromator (20ID-MN-2)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: An optional second monochromator that narrows the energy spread 10 to 1,000 times further, as very-far-field strain mapping and coherent imaging require. Four flat silicon crystals steer the beam up and back down again (a +−−+ arrangement), so it leaves on its original line. The common Si(111) reflection gives a spread of about 10⁻⁴; higher-order reflections reach 10⁻⁵ to 10⁻⁶, for coherent imaging of grains about 10 µm across. The crystal pairs sit on flexure mounts, in air, following a design proven at 1-ID.

components.name: Attenuators F2 and calibration foils F3
components.distanceNote: Approximate: from FDR Fig. 4.19, between M2 and L3; not listed in Table 4.28.
components.text: Rotating wheels slide metal sheets into the beam, either to dim it or to check its exact energy against the absorption edges of chemical elements, energies at which an element suddenly absorbs much more strongly. The foils also reveal any drift in energy during long experiments; both designs were proven at 1-ID.

components.name: Monochromatic slits S2
components.distanceNote: Approximate: drawn between foils F3 and lenses L3 in FDR Fig. 4.19; not listed in FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: Adjustable metal jaws that trim the single-energy beam just after the monochromators, before the last lenses in the optics enclosure. Like HEXM's other monochromatic slits, they sit on stages that are aligned to the beam once and then left in place.

components.name: L3 long-focal-length focusing / beam-expanding lenses
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28, where the lenses are marked 'not in project scope'; the PDR quotes about 34 m.
components.text: Lenses that either gently focus the beam into the far stations, to 155 × 40 µm at 20-ID-E (70 keV, design), or spread it into a wide, even beam big enough to image a whole sample at once. For spreading, diamond lenses shaped to diverge the beam turn a width of about 0.5 mm here into 3–4 mm after 180 m, the wide beam that near-field grain mapping and CT need. A 2026 paper reports a proof-of-principle test of such diamond expanders, though how they are used here is unverified.

components.name: Be window, photon mask and tungsten collimator (20ID-WN-2, PM-1, BC-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28 (window 33.9 m, mask 34.0 m, collimator 34.4 m).
components.text: Radiation-safety hardware at the end of the optics enclosure: a beryllium window, a mask and a tungsten collimator keep the beam inside its pipe and block stray high-energy radiation from the accelerator. Because HEXM can run white beam with a direct line of sight to the source, such mask-and-collimator pairs repeat along the line, narrowing the cone of bremsstrahlung step by step.

components.name: White-beam / bremsstrahlung shutter (P4-80)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: The main door for the beam: when this shutter is closed, people can safely enter the experiment stations downstream. It works in white-beam or monochromatic mode and also blocks bremsstrahlung, the high-energy radiation from the accelerator.

components.name: Shielded white-beam transport ST-1 (through legacy 20-ID-B/C)
components.distanceNote: Exact span 36.0–65.3 m (FDR Table 4.28).
components.text: A lead-shielded vacuum pipe that carries the beam about 30 m across the experiment hall, straight through two older hutches, 20-ID-B and 20-ID-C, which remain standing but are no longer used. It is rated for the full white beam.

components.name: 20-ID-D entrance: mask, collimator, Be window (PM-2, BC-2)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28 (66.2, 66.5 and 66.8 m).
components.text: More radiation-safety hardware where the beam enters the first experiment hutch, 20-ID-D: a photon mask, a tungsten collimator and a beryllium window within 0.6 m of each other. Together they make sure only the intended beam enters the hutch.

components.name: Multi-beam slits S3 (20ID-SL-3)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: Motorised jaws that shape the beam. Closed down, they act as a tiny stand-in source (a secondary source), so the lenses downstream make a steadier focus, and they can tune how coherent the beam is across its width.

components.name: Fast shutter (20ID-FS-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: A fast shutter, like a camera's, that times each X-ray exposure exactly. It opens only while the detector is recording.

components.name: L4 short-focal-length focusing optics
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28, where the lenses are marked 'not in project scope'.
components.text: Strong lenses, with focal lengths under 2 m, that squeeze the beam to about a micrometre, a hundredth of the width of a hair, for experiments in 20-ID-D: 0.96 × 0.87 µm with 2.7 × 10¹² photons per second at 70 keV in the design. Candidates include silicon saw-tooth lenses, whose focal length can be tuned continuously, and kinoform lenses, refractive lenses with the excess material cut away, which reached 230 nm at 51 keV in tests at 1-ID.

components.name: Multi-beam slits S4 (20ID-SL-4)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: Motorised clean-up slits just before the sample in 20-ID-D that trim away stray X-rays. They can also define the beam or tune its coherence.

components.name: High-throughput HEDM instrument (20-ID-D)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28 (20ID-BI-1 instrumentation). The 3D model shows 20-ID-D idle, with no sample mounted, passing the beam on to 20-ID-E (schematic).
components.text: A grain-mapping machine built by four universities with National Science Foundation funding. Its six-axis motorised stage turns and steps each sample through the beam, so many samples can be measured quickly: an assembly line for 3D crystal maps. It moved here from 6-ID-D in December 2023, and 20-ID-D also hosts in situ white-beam experiments. In this scene it stands idle, with no sample mounted, while the beam travels on to 20-ID-E.

components.name: 20-ID-D area detector(s)
components.distanceNote: Exact span 72.5–75 m (FDR Table 4.28). The 3D model shows it moved 0.7 m inboard, out of the beam that continues to 20-ID-E (schematic).
components.text: A large flat-panel X-ray camera, 2–5 m behind the sample, that records the sharp diffraction spots thrown off by each crystal grain. The design called for a Dexela 2923 or equivalent; the beamline directory lists Varex 4343 and SpectrumLogic 3131HS detectors without saying which station uses which. In this scene it is moved aside so the beam can pass to the far station.

components.name: Multi-beam slits S5 (20ID-SL-5)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: An aperture that picks out the part of the beam sent on toward the far station. For coherent imaging it selects the central patch of the beam across which the waves are in step, before the L5 lenses.

components.name: L5 long-focal-length lenses (focus into 20-ID-E)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28, where the lenses are marked 'not in project scope'.
components.text: Gentle lenses that aim a focus about 100 m away, in the far experiment room, re-imaging the source roughly one to one into a broad beam whose waves stay in step across it, for coherent imaging. With focal lengths of 104 m vertically (working with the L2 lenses) and 44 m horizontally, the design gives a 48 × 31 µm spot at 40 keV, or 48 × 13 µm with 6.5 × 10¹³ photons per second at 70 keV.

components.name: Movable white/bremsstrahlung beam stop (20ID-BS-1)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28. Drawn raised (open), so the beam continues to 20-ID-E.
components.text: A cooled, movable stop for white or monochromatic beam. Closed, it ends the beam here, so experiments can run in 20-ID-D while people work in 20-ID-E; open, it lets the beam fly on to the far station.

components.name: Long shielded transport ST-2 (hall to Long Beamline Building)
components.distanceNote: Exact span 77.0–177.5 m (FDR Table 4.28).
components.enclosure: transport (LOM 436 and the HEXM corridor of the LBB)
components.text: A 100 m lead-shielded vacuum pipe that leaves the experiment hall, passes through a lab-office building and along a new corridor of 14 offices, and enters the Long Beamline Building. With the first transport pipe it adds up to about 140 m of shielded white-beam transport. People now cross it on new stairs and an elevator, which ended the tradition of walking all the way round the ring.

components.name: 20-ID-E entrance window and white-beam slits (WN-4, SL-7)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28 (window 177.7 m; slits 178.2 m, marked 'TEMP').
components.text: The beam enters the giant end station, 20-ID-E, through a window, and portable slits trim it once more. They are built for white beam, because broadband beams focused by the white-beam lenses can concentrate a lot of power.

components.name: Beam-conditioning optics table with L6 nano-focusing lenses
components.distanceNote: Exact for L6 (FDR Table 4.28); the table spans about 178–180 m (approximate).
components.text: A long, very stable table carrying the final lenses, slits, beam monitors and a fast shutter. Its lenses, with focal lengths of 1–2 m, can squeeze the X-rays to a spot designed to be 0.43 × 0.21 µm at 70 keV, about 200 nm tall, two metres away at the sample. Three effects of similar size set that height: the shrunken image of the source (99 nm), blur from the beam's spread of energies (152 nm) and diffraction (104 nm), which combine to 209 nm. A 1 m kinoform lens with a narrower energy spread could reach 77 nm.

specs.vertical spot budget (f = 2 m): 99 nm source, 152 nm chromatic, 104 nm diffraction → 209 nm

components.name: Be window 20ID-WN-5 (temporary)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28 ('Window Be (TEMP)'), at the downstream end of the beam-conditioning table.
components.text: A thin beryllium window, 70 cm before the sample, where the vacuum pipe ends. The X-rays cross the last stretch in air, so bulky furnaces and load frames can sit right in the beam; evacuated flight tubes with an extra cooled window can close the air gap, especially for white beam. The window is listed as temporary.

components.name: Sample position: HR-SMS, HL-SMS and RAMS load frame
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28 (20ID-BI-3). ESD-010 places the origin 3.5 m from the upstream wall, 1.4 m above the floor. The 3D model shows the high-load stage with a load frame at the beam and the high-resolution stage (hexapod with the rotation stage on top, as in the poster rendering) parked inboard on the exchange rails; rail, truss and cart dimensions are schematic.
components.text: The one spot where every technique meets: a single calibrated sample position, 180.7 m from the source and 1.4 m above the floor, shared by all the detectors. Two sample stages swap in on floor rails: a high-resolution stage, a hexapod topped by a rotation stage, and a high-load cart with guide columns for load frames. Rigs stretch, twist, heat or cycle the sample while the X-rays look inside, among them the RAMS rotational and axial load frame, a radio-frequency furnace and a battery cycler.

components.name: D1 near-field / imaging detector
components.distanceNote: Approximate: 1–2 cm behind the sample for nf-HEDM (PDR), further downstream for µCT. The 3D model shows it retracted about 0.1 m outboard of the beam, as in a far-field measurement (schematic).
components.text: A high-resolution camera almost touching the sample, 1–2 cm behind it, for near-field grain mapping and CT. A thin crystal screen (a scintillator) turns X-rays into visible light, which a mirror and microscope lens pass to a camera, giving about 1 µm resolution. The catch is efficiency: such a thin screen stops less than 10% of X-rays above 40 keV, so better detectors are still being developed.

components.name: D2 detector system (near far-field WAXS/HEDM)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: about 1 m behind the sample, inferred from the PDR concept and the poster rendering. The 3D model shows it moved about 0.8 m inboard, out of the direct beam, as when the far-field detectors are in use (schematic).
components.text: A large flat-panel camera on a six-legged robotic mount (a hexapod), about a metre behind the sample, that catches the diffraction rings from thousands of grains at once, for wide-angle scattering and far-field grain mapping. In this scene it is moved aside so the far detectors can see.

components.name: L7 TXM objective (direct or diffracted beam)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: the PDR places L7 'after the sample' and the poster shows a TXM objective stand in the downstream hutch; the exact distance is unpublished. The 3D model shows it lowered out of the beam on its lift (schematic).
components.text: An X-ray lens after the sample that acts as a microscope objective, projecting a magnified image onto a camera at the back of the room. Placed in the direct beam it serves transmission microscopy, aiming at about 100 nm; placed in the beam diffracted by one grain, it images only that grain (dark-field microscopy). It can also relay far-field patterns to the back-wall detectors.

components.name: D3 detector manipulation system (2–12 m WAXS / HEDM)
components.distanceNote: Exact rail range: Z = 183–193 m (ESD-010); FDR Table 4.28 gives 183.3–192.5 m. Listed at the upstream end of its travel; the 3D model shows it 6 m from the sample on the outboard rail, catching a Debye ring at 2θ = 8° (schematic configuration).
components.text: A tower that carries a 100 kg detector on floor rails 2–12 m behind the sample and moves it metres sideways and up, to catch diffraction anywhere in a cone 36° wide: scattering angles up to 18°, enough to see atomic spacings down to 1 Å at 40 keV. It must return to a position within 75 µm and drift less than 15 µm a day, watched by a laser tracker. The design's reference detector is a Pilatus3 X CdTe 6M, and the original robot-arm concept became this floor-rail tower.

components.name: D6 SAXS detector
components.distanceNote: Approximate: about 14 m from the sample (PDR); the SAXS table is near the back wall in ESD Fig. 2.
components.text: A camera about 14 m behind the sample that catches X-rays deflected by only tiny angles, revealing nanometre-sized pores and particles. It reaches a smallest scattering vector of 0.0007 Å⁻¹ at 40 keV, enough for structures up to about 870 nm. The design concept called for a photon-counting detector.

components.name: D5 TXM imaging detector
components.distanceNote: Approximate: about 15 m from the sample (PDR). D5 and D6 share the axis near the back wall; the 3D model shows D5 moved 1.3 m inboard (schematic).
components.text: The 'projection screen' for the X-ray microscope: the camera, about 15 m from the sample, where the lens's magnified image lands. It needs high resolution and high efficiency at high energies; one vendor reports amorphous-selenium detectors with 8 µm pixels 'designed into' the new beamline, without saying which position they serve.

specs.candidate: KA Imaging BrillianSe a-Se, 8 µm pixels (vendor statement)

components.name: D4 back-wall detector system (BCDI / vff-HEDM)
components.distanceNote: Approximate: 'approximately 197 m' (ESD-010). The 3D model shows it on the back wall catching a single Bragg spot at 2θ = 8°, 2.3 m off axis (schematic configuration).
components.text: A detector that travels across the back wall, about 16 m from the sample. That far away, diffraction spots spread out, so the tiniest changes in angle, and the speckle pattern of a single grain, become visible. The upper half of the 17.8° diffraction cone reaches the wall, including pairs of opposite reflections (Friedel pairs). Sampling coherent-imaging fringes finely enough needs a detector with 5 µm resolution or better, high efficiency and a wide dynamic range, still a development goal.

specs.resolution requirement: ≤ 5 µm, high efficiency and dynamic range (R&D)

components.name: Fixed white-beam stop (20ID-BS-2)
components.distanceNote: Exact: FDR Table 4.28.
components.text: The end of the line, 197 m from the source: a cooled block at the back wall that safely absorbs whatever is left of the white or monochromatic beam.

enclosures.role: former spectroscopy hutch; beam passes through in shielded pipe

Beam 1.4 m above floor, 5.4 m from the outboard wall in the wide section. Doorways on both sides at about 185 m. Floor slab 12 in. A yellow bridge crane with chain hoist spans the tall downstream section (MPE panorama photo, Jan 2024); ESD Fig. 2 marks a crane-runway level at the top of the low upstream section. The LBB exists to give long-distance optics, low-background environments and better stability.

instruments.name: High-Throughput HEDM instrument (HT-HEDM)
instruments.text: An 'assembly-line' grain-mapping station in 20-ID-D, built by four universities led by Carnegie Mellon with a National Science Foundation instrumentation grant (about $1.09 million obligated), and moved to HEXM in December 2023. A six-axis Aerotech stage handles samples in white or monochromatic beam for far-field grain mapping, wide-angle scattering and imaging. It is built for high throughput, potentially including mail-in samples.
detectors: Varex 4343 / SpectrumLogic 3131HS (Beamline Directory; station not specified)

instruments.name: 20-ID-E multi-modal end-station instrument
instruments.text: A room-sized X-ray microscope: one sample position, two interchangeable sample stages and detectors from a centimetre or two to 16 m away, so users can switch between 3D grain maps, CT scans, nanoscale scattering and coherent imaging without moving the sample. A beam-conditioning table delivers the final focus; a high-resolution hexapod stage and a high-load cart for load frames run on floor rails under an overhead truss, and a laser tracker keeps track of the detectors. Six detector systems cover near-field (D1), far-field (D2, D3), back-wall (D4), microscope (D5) and small-angle (D6) work. The hutch is designed to hold its temperature to ±0.05 °C over 24 hours, on a floor built to a strict vibration standard (VC-E).
detectors: D3 large-area detector on DMS (Pilatus3 X CdTe 6M used as the spec reference)
KA Imaging BrillianSe a-Se (8 µm pixel; vendor claim 'designed into' 20-ID; position not stated)
sampleEnvironments: RAMS rotational and axial motion load frame
Psylotech µTS / xTS 5 kN load frames (AML)

instruments.name: Activated Materials Laboratory (support facility)
instruments.text: A safe workshop for radioactive samples right next to the X-ray hutch, with fume hoods, shielded glove boxes and equipment to seal samples in containers. Funded through the Department of Energy's Nuclear Science User Facilities (NSUF), it accepts samples giving up to 100 millirem per hour at 30 cm and transports them to 1-ID and 20-ID. NSUF holds 690 hours a year of beam time through a partner user proposal.

geometryNotes:
HEXM follows a single straight line from the 20-ID straight section to the fixed stop at 197 m, with no net horizontal deflection. The bent double-Laue M1 (29.5 m) displaces the monochromatic beam 25–35 mm outboard and parallel; white-beam operation runs on axis. The four-bounce M2 has zero net offset. The beam is tangent to the ring at sector 20, so the line leaves the hall at a slight angle to its neighbors. The ISN (19-ID) line starts about 2 m inboard but is rotated 9° outboard, so in the Long Beamline Building ISN lies on HEXM's outboard side. Outboard means the left of the beam direction, APS +X (ESD-010; site.json gives a 20-ID direction of 168.8° vs 177.8° for 19-ID in site coordinates).

Inside the hall: 20-ID-A against the ratchet wall (about 26–36 m), a shielded pipe through the unused legacy 20-ID-B and -C hutches (about 50–65 m), then the new 20-ID-D (about 65–77 m) as far downstream as the hall allows.

The roughly 100 m ST-2 pipe crosses the experiment-floor walkway (stairs and an elevator lift people over it), passes through LOM Bldg 436, where offices were removed, and runs along a new office corridor into Bldg 444, the LBB.

20-ID-E is a two-level lead hutch. The upstream third is low: 6.8 m wide, about 4 m high, with a roof walkway. The downstream part, from about 188.8 m, is wide and tall (10.8 × 6.9 m), so the 2θ = 17.8° Debye cone (1 Å at 40 keV) can reach the back-wall D4 detector about 16 m from the sample. Check: tan(17.8°) × 16.4 m = 5.3 m, against 5.4 m to the side walls and 5.5 m from beam height to the ceiling. The beam is 1.4 m above the floor.

On the as-built poster an overhead truss bridges the sample area; D3 and D4 are tall tan pillar-type movers labeled 'HEXM'. The AML is on the inboard side of 20-ID-E. The control room and sample prep were drawn on the outboard side in 2019.

Outside, the LBB massing reads AML (low) – HEXM (tall) – ISN (Strategic Plan photo).

The FDR Fig. 4.1 caption says the beam travels left to right, but in that drawing the APS ring is at the right and the LBB at the left, so the beam actually runs right to left. Read that way, HEXM is inboard of ISN and the AML is inboard of HEXM, consistent with FDR Fig. 4.18 (beam left to right: control room and sample prep drawn above, i.e. outboard; AML below, i.e. inboard).

interactiveIdeas.title: Zoom-in, zoom-out
interactiveIdeas.concept: Start with a jet-engine turbine blade, then scroll through powers of ten. At each step the exhibit switches technique and detector distance on the 3D hutch model: µCT (mm, beam size/1000), nf-HEDM grain map (µm), ff-HEDM strain per grain, BCDI or DFXM inside one grain (tens of nm), and WAXS/PDF d-spacings (sub-A).
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: No single image covers 7 orders of magnitude. HEXM combines techniques at one sample position so each scale guides where to zoom next.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Direct imaging resolution is roughly beam size/1000. Grain-resolved HEDM works for up to about 10⁴ grains in the beam. nf-HEDM resolves about 1 µm and 0.01°. ff-HEDM gives about 2 × 10⁻⁴ strain per grain. BCDI resolves tens of nm with strain about 10⁻⁴. Keep 2θ under about 10–18° at 35–120 keV.

interactiveIdeas.title: X-ray vision vs energy
interactiveIdeas.concept: Slider from 10 to 120 keV with slabs of Al, Ti, steel, Ni superalloy, W. Show the transmitted beam and a 'see-through depth' gauge, and overlay a turbine blade, a battery and a reactor fuel pellet.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why HEXM needs high energy: the X-rays have to pass through real-size metal parts and their containment.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Use NIST mass attenuation coefficients: I/I₀ = exp(−(µ/ρ)ρt). Fe 1/e length is about 7 µm at 10 keV, 0.35 mm at 40 keV, about 1.5 mm at 70 keV and 3.4 mm at 100 keV. W and U stay strongly absorbing: the AML report puts their penetration near 100 µm at 70 keV and above. Computed NIST values span roughly 0.03–0.25 mm over 40–120 keV, with jumps at the W (69.5 keV) and U (115.6 keV) K edges. Show the W K-edge (69.5 keV) jump. Attenuation is not linear in E.

interactiveIdeas.title: Why 180 meters? Build your own focus
interactiveIdeas.concept: Drag a lens along the beam (D station at 70 m, E station at 180 m) and choose f. Live readout of the spot size as source demag (+) chromatic aberration (+) diffraction limit, and a toggle between brightness and timing source modes. A second mode turns the lens into a beam expander.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Distance helps both ways: smaller spots at a convenient working distance, and wide, uniform beams for whole-sample imaging.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Thin lens 1/f = 1/p + 1/q; demagnified size = 2.355 σ(source) × q/p. FWHM terms add in quadrature: at 180 m, f = 2 m, 70 keV, 99 + 152 + 104 nm gives 209 nm (V, FDR Table 4.30). CRL focal length f = R/(2N δ); for diamond at 70 keV δ is about 1.5 × 10⁻⁷ (computed from electron density), so R = 50 µm needs N of about 84 for f = 2 m. Focal length scales as E² (δ proportional to λ²), so chromatic blur scales with ΔE/E. Kinoforms beat CRLs on aperture.

interactiveIdeas.title: Move the detector: near, far, very far
interactiveIdeas.concept: One polycrystal and one rotating sample. Slide the detector from 1 cm (nf) to 1 m (ff) to 15 m (vff). Spots spread out, position information fades and strain resolution sharpens. Then apply load and watch individual spots shift.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: The same diffraction carries different information depending on distance, and HEXM's 20 m hutch makes the 'very far' mode possible.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Bragg's law: λ = 2 d sin(θ), λ[Å] = 12.398/E[keV]. Fe(110) at 70 keV has 2θ of about 5.0°. Strain Δd/d = −cot θ Δθ, and angular resolution is about pixel/L. Near field (1–2 cm) gives spatial maps; far field gives grain averages.

interactiveIdeas.title: Coherence and the speckle pattern of one grain (BCDI)
interactiveIdeas.concept: Compare old APS and APS-U source sizes. Show the coherence patch at 180 m, then illuminate one grain and show its 3D speckle. A detector-pixel slider reveals when fringes become undersampled, and a bandwidth slider shows fringes washing out unless ΔE/E is 10⁻⁵ or below.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Coherent imaging at high energy needed the upgrade, a very monochromatic beam and a very long hutch.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Gaussian Schell model: rms transverse coherence length ξ = λ z/(2 π σ). At 40 keV, 180 m, ξx is about 60 µm (APS-U, σx 14.5 µm) vs about 3 µm (old APS, 280 µm); this is computed, and conventions differ by factors of about 2. Longitudinal coherence is about λ/(2 ΔE/E); at 40 keV (λ = 0.31 Å) that is about 15 nm at 10⁻³, 1.5 µm at 10⁻⁵ and 7.8 µm at 2 × 10⁻⁶ (computed; some authors use λ²/Δλ, twice as long). Fringe period on the detector is λ L/D, about 50 µm for D = 10 µm, L = 16 m at 40 keV, so pixels need to be 25 µm or less. Design coherent focus is 48 × 31 µm (FDR Fig. 4.20).

interactiveIdeas.title: Undulator harmonic ladder
interactiveIdeas.concept: Pick the current U21 or the future 16.5 mm SCU and drag K (the gap or current). Odd harmonics slide across 35–120 keV, and a metre shows how many harmonics overlap a chosen energy and how bright each is.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: High-energy beamlines run on high undulator harmonics. Shorter periods and stronger fields (superconducting magnets) put more photons where HEXM works.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Eₙ[keV] = n × 0.9496 Eₑ[GeV]² / (λu[cm] (1 + K²/2)) with Eₑ = 6.0 GeV. U21: E1 = 8.36 keV at K = 1.38, so 70 keV is about the 7th harmonic at K of about 1.1 (computed). Only odd harmonics on axis. The 0.136% electron energy spread broadens high harmonics strongly (Tanaka-Kitamura factor at n × N × σE). Planned SCU vs pre-upgrade SCU1: 530× brilliance.

interactiveIdeas.title: Why the hutch looks like a step pyramid
interactiveIdeas.concept: Cutaway of 20-ID-E. Light up the 1 Å, 40 keV Debye cone from the sample and watch it fill the tall, wide back half and hit the D4 wall. A slider changes the energy or d-spacing and the cone shrinks or grows.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Building shapes follow physics: the back half is 10.8 m wide and 6.9 m tall so an 18° cone fits.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: 2θ = 2 asin(λ/2d) is 17.8° for d = 1 Å at 40 keV. Radius = L tan(2θ) is about 5.3 m at L of about 16.4 m. Beam height 1.4 m, so only the upper half-cone reaches the wall.

interactiveIdeas.title: Ride along with a radioactive sample
interactiveIdeas.concept: Step-by-step journey: reactor component, then shipping cask, AML glove box, encapsulation, transfer cart to 20-ID-E, HEDM scan and return. Dose-rate counters update along the way.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: How a long beamline and a dedicated lab make it safe to study irradiated materials with X-rays.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Limit 100 mrem/h beta/gamma at 30 cm. At least one containment layer. Containment walls must be X-ray transparent at 60–100 keV; the 1/e length is about mm in steel and Zr. Higher-dose samples go preferentially to 20-ID, outside the main hall.

funFacts: At about 20 m long, 20-ID-E is 'the largest enclosure we've built at the APS'.
HEXM's main hutch stands in its own building, the Long Beamline Building. Its groundbreaking on July 22, 2020 was described as 'the only externally visible part of the APS Upgrade'.
The X-rays travel about 180 m (590 ft) to the sample, roughly 2.3 times the 'more typical 80 meters', and arrive about 0.6 microseconds after leaving the electron beam (travel time computed).
Building HEXM meant removing offices in lab-office Building 436 and adding a new corridor of 14 offices along the beam pipe.
The long beamlines cut the walkway around the APS ring at sectors 19–20. Stairs and an elevator now carry people over the beam pipes, ending the tradition of a full lap on foot or tricycle.
The back half of 20-ID-E is 10.8 m wide and 6.9 m tall so that X-rays scattered at 18 degrees can still land on a detector 16 m away.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright placed HEXM's inaugural sample, a piece of a jet-engine turbine blade, in July 2025.
The high-throughput HEDM instrument in 20-ID-D was built by four universities with NSF funding: 'many places with wading pools... this instrument... will be an Olympic swimming pool'.

Before HEXM, sector 20 hosted X-ray spectroscopy for more than 25 years (about 600 papers). That program moved to 25-ID in 2022, and the sector's history goes back to the Pacific Northwest Consortium CAT formed in 1990.
HEXM's hutch sits on a 12-inch concrete slab; its long-beamline neighbor ISN needed 39 inches for vibration control.
Next door is a lab built to handle radioactive samples; its first users studied stainless-steel parts retired from a nuclear reactor after decades of service.
Before the upgrade, only about 1 in 100,000 photons at HEDM energies was spatially coherent, which made high-energy coherent imaging impractical.
'HEXM will be the only beamline worldwide to offer dark-field X-ray microscopy at high energies' (Ashley Bucsek, University of Michigan).
The design calls for a laser tracker (Leica Absolute Tracker class) to watch where the 100 kg detectors are inside the hutch.

openQuestions: The exact first-light date is not published. Monthly charts show stage 2 (installation complete) in December 2024 and January 2025, stage 3 (operations commissioning) on 10 March 2025 and stage 5 by July 2025, and the July 2025 AML report says shielding verification happened 'in 2025'. First light is therefore bracketed between late January and July 2025, most likely by March 2025.
Status conflict: the 5 Oct 2026 chart shows stage 6 (general users) and the Proposal Types page lists 20-ID-D,E for GU proposals, but the Beamline Directory still says 'Commissioning' (likely stale).

Source: interim permanent-magnet U21 + U21/U25 revolver as of 22 Sep 2026. The SCU baseline changed from about 3.5–3.8 m total (FDR 4-4, Kmax 1.63) to 2 × 1.9 m in one cryostat (FDR Ch3, Strategic Plan). Installation is planned for 2026–2027 after core-reliability problems. The Beamline Directory specs (10¹⁴ ph/s at 70 keV) assume the SCU and have not been measured with the interim source.
Front-end window material: 0.5 mm Be (FDR 4-4.3 and the Table 4.27 note) vs 'Diamond Window' (FDR Table 4.28). As-built not confirmed.

Which refractive optics (L1–L7) are installed as of 2026 is unclear. The FDR lists most lens sets as 'Not in Project Scope' (R&D), and the AML report (July 2025) confirms 'refractive-based focusing optics' in 20-ID-A without details. Shastri & Antipov (JSR 2026) describe diamond lenses for collimation into a high-resolution monochromator, focusing for coherent diffraction 'on a long beamline' and a convex beam-expander test at 40–70 keV (abstract via Europe PMC). The full text is Cloudflare-blocked, so lens positions, focal lengths and the beamline used are unverified.

As-built detector suite: the Directory lists a Varex 4343 and a SpectrumLogic 3131HS (station not specified). The D3 specification used a Pilatus3 X CdTe 6M as reference, KA Imaging claims BrillianSe a-Se detectors, and D4 (ESD-011) details are unpublished. 'SpectrumLogic 3131HS' specs could not be verified.
BCDI and DFXM operational status for users is unknown: the AML report lists BCDI as available at 20-ID-E, but no published HEXM BCDI/DFXM result was found.
The 2017 PDR XMAT in situ ion-irradiation source ('20–30 m of space' next to the C/E station) is not mentioned in later documents; presumably not built.

Enclosure extents for 20-ID-A, -B, -C and -D were scaled from the 2019 FDR layout figure (about ±0.5 m) and may differ from as-built. 20-ID-E dimensions come from the 2021 ESD and match the 64'-11" × 35'-5" in FDR Fig. 4.1.
Sample position: 180.7 m (FDR Table 4.28) vs about 180.9 m implied by ESD-010 (3.5 m from the upstream wall at about 177.4 m).
Upper energy limit: 120 keV (FDR, Directory) vs 140 keV (D3 ESD photon-delivery statement).
Station naming changed: the PDR (2017) used A/B/C; the FDR and as-built use 20-ID-A, -D and -E. Legacy 20-ID-B/C remain in the hall but are unused.
The beamline used for the first AML user experiment (Feb 2026 DOE article) was not stated: 1-ID or 20-ID.
FDR Table 4.29 labels all beam sizes as µm, but the 'unfocused' rows (2.5 × 2.2 at E; 1 × 0.9 at D) must be mm (confirmed by the Beamline Directory).

The 3D model shows one consistent snapshot: 20-ID-E running far-field HEDM at 70 keV while 20-ID-D passes the beam through (no sample mounted, detector moved aside). Real stations alternate; 20-ID-D can run on its own with the movable stop closed.
